blocks.text: On the first morning of a respiratory outpatient placement, a student is told she cannot join the clinic: her occupational health clearance has not been received. A week later, having finally been cleared, she arrives with no particular aims and spends the day 'just watching'. Both problems were avoidable, and both were decided before she set foot in the building.

blocks.markdown: A shadowing placement is short, and supervisors are busy. How much you learn depends largely on what you do **beforehand**. This unit covers three parts of preparation: setting **specific learning goals**, completing the **occupational health and mandatory training requirements** that must be in place before clinical contact, and preparing **questions** that make the best use of a supervisor's limited time.

blocks.title: Shadowing
blocks.text: **Shadowing** is learning by observing a clinician or team at work, with limited and closely supervised participation. Because you are not responsible for patient care, your learning has to be driven by your own goals and questions.

blocks.markdown:
### Setting specific learning goals

Vague aims such as 'see how a clinic works' give you nothing to aim at and nothing to review afterwards. Good goals are **SMART**: **S**pecific, **M**easurable, **A**chievable, **R**elevant and **T**ime-bound. Link them to your curriculum (for example, the history-taking, examination and professionalism outcomes of your course) and to the setting you are visiting. Aim for **three to five** goals, mixing knowledge, skills and professional behaviours, and share them with your supervisor early, so they can help you meet them or tell you which are unrealistic.

blocks.caption: Turning vague aims into SMART goals
rows: Learn about asthma
By the end of the week, take and present two histories from patients with wheeze and describe how peak flow monitoring is used
Specific outputs and a deadline
Get better at examinations
Perform and be observed doing a respiratory examination on at least three patients, and obtain feedback on technique after each
Measurable number and feedback built in
See a busy clinic
Describe in a 200-word reflection how the clinic team manages the order and flow of patients and how handover occurs
Produces something that can be reviewed
Be professional
Introduce myself with name and role to every patient and staff member I meet, and ask my supervisor at the end of day 2 whether I did this consistently
Observable behaviour checked by someone else

blocks.title: Writing SMART goals for a placement
blocks.prompt: You will spend five days in a diabetes outpatient clinic. Your vague aim is 'learn about diabetes'. Write two SMART goals, one for knowledge and one for a clinical skill, and say how each will be reviewed.

steps.text: Knowledge goal, specific: explain in my own words how the clinic team decides whether a patient's blood glucose control is adequate, and the common complications they screen for.
Make it measurable and time-bound: write a one-page summary by Wednesday and discuss it with my supervisor for 5 minutes on Thursday.
Skill goal, specific: take a focused history from at least two patients with diabetes, covering symptoms, medications, self-monitoring and lifestyle, by the end of day 4, under supervision.
Make it measurable and reviewable: ask the supervisor for feedback after each history and record one action from each, then review whether those actions were applied in the second history.

Check achievability and relevance: confirm with the supervisor that patients are willing and there is time in clinic, and that the goals map to the course outcomes on history-taking and long-term conditions.

blocks.answer: A SMART goal states what you will do, how it will be measured, by when, and how it will be reviewed, within what the placement allows.

blocks.markdown:
### Requirements before clinical contact

Before you meet patients, your university and the host organisation must be satisfied that you are **safe to be near patients** and that patients are **safe near you**. Exact requirements are set by your medical school and the host trust, so always follow their current checklist. Typically they include the following.

blocks.caption: Typical pre-placement requirements in the UK
rows: Occupational health clearance
Protect patients and you from infection and confirm fitness for the role
Health questionnaire, immunisation records, infection screening as required
Immunisations and screening
Reduce the risk of infections spreading in healthcare settings
Hepatitis B, MMR (measles, mumps, rubella), varicella (chickenpox) immunity, tuberculosis assessment, and blood-borne virus screening before exposure-prone procedures, per current national guidance
Disclosure and barring check
Safeguard children and vulnerable adults
An enhanced DBS check or equivalent for your nation, renewed as required
Mandatory training
Ensure baseline safety knowledge
Infection prevention and control, hand hygiene, manual handling, fire safety, information governance and confidentiality, safeguarding, basic life support as required locally
Identification and dress code
Identify you and meet infection-control rules
Visible ID badge, bare below the elbows, clean uniform or smart dress, tied-back hair
Insurance, indemnity and local induction
Clarify cover and local rules
Medical school indemnity, host site induction, emergency procedures and contacts

blocks.title: No clearance, no contact
blocks.text: If occupational health clearance or mandatory training is incomplete, you may be refused patient contact, however well prepared you are otherwise. Start early because immunisation courses and results can take weeks to complete.

blocks.title: Working back from a start date
blocks.prompt: Your placement in an elderly care ward starts in five weeks. Your occupational health record shows that you have not completed your hepatitis B vaccination course and your information governance training has expired. You have not received your ward induction details. List the order in which you would act and why.

steps.text: Contact occupational health first, because immunisation courses take time and a gap may prevent clinical contact. Ask what evidence they need and the earliest appointment.
Complete the online information governance and other mandatory training, since these can be done quickly and the certificates are usually required before day one.
Email the placement office or ward contact to request the induction, dress code, start time, parking or entry details and the name of your supervisor.
Once cleared, send your supervisor your goals and ask when they are free to discuss them early in the week.
Keep copies of certificates and clearance letters, and bring identification on the first day.

blocks.answer: Start with occupational health because of lead times, then mandatory training, then logistics and supervisor contact, keeping evidence of completion.

blocks.markdown:
### Questions that make the best use of a supervisor's time

Supervisors are often managing patients while teaching you. **Prepare** by reading about the common conditions in that setting, noting what you do not understand, and writing questions down. Then:

- Ask **specific, open** questions ('How do you decide when to start insulin rather than adding another tablet?') rather than 'Can you tell me about diabetes?'
- Prioritise: choose the two or three most valuable questions, and **batch** the rest for a scheduled slot at the end of a session.
- Ask the right person: practical questions to the nurse or clinic administrator; clinical reasoning questions to the doctor.
- Pick your moment: not during a patient consultation, an emergency or documentation.
- Show what you already know ('I think this is X because of Y; is that right?'), so the supervisor can correct or extend rather than start from scratch.

blocks.caption: Weak and strong questions
rows: What is heart failure?
In today's clinic, why did you choose a loop diuretic rather than increasing the dose of the other tablet?
Targets reasoning in a real case
Can I ask a question?
When you have 5 minutes after clinic, could I check my understanding of the examination I saw?
States the content and timing
Why did you not do an ECG?
What made an ECG unnecessary for this patient?
Avoids sounding critical and invites explanation
Where is the form?
Ask the ward clerk or nurse
Right person for practical matters

points: Set three to five SMART goals before you start, link them to your course outcomes, and share them with your supervisor early.
Complete occupational health clearance, immunisations and screening, DBS and mandatory training before clinical contact, and begin early because some steps take weeks.
Prepare specific, open, prioritised questions, ask the right person at a suitable time, and show what you already know.

questions.stem: Which of the following is the best example of a SMART learning goal for a one-week placement?

options.text: Take and present two histories from patients with chest symptoms by Thursday, and obtain feedback from my supervisor after each
Learn about the heart
Do well on the placement
Watch as many consultations as possible

questions.correctOptionText: Take and present two histories from patients with chest symptoms by Thursday, and obtain feedback from my supervisor after each

distractorRationale.a: Correct: specific, measurable, time-bound and linked to feedback.
distractorRationale.b: Too vague to measure or review.
distractorRationale.d: Not specific or learning-focused, and does not say how to measure.

questions.explanation: SMART goals say exactly what you will do, how it can be checked and by when. The correct option names a task, a number, a deadline and a feedback step.

questions.stem: A student's goal is 'be more confident on the ward'. Which change makes it more measurable?

options.text: Introduce myself with name and role to every new patient on days 1 to 3 and ask my supervisor to confirm I did so
Try to feel more confident
Avoid situations that make me nervous
Keep a mental note of how I feel

questions.correctOptionText: Introduce myself with name and role to every new patient on days 1 to 3 and ask my supervisor to confirm I did so

distractorRationale.a: Correct: observable behaviour, time frame and external check.
distractorRationale.b: A restatement of the aim, not measurable.
distractorRationale.d: Mental notes cannot be reviewed objectively.

questions.explanation: Turning a feeling into an observable behaviour with a time frame and an external check makes it measurable. Confidence then follows from repeated, observed practice.

questions.stem: Which of the following is a typical requirement to be completed before a student has contact with patients on a UK placement?

options.text: Occupational health clearance, including immunisation and screening records, and mandatory training such as infection control
A written examination on surgical techniques
Purchase of a personal stethoscope from the host hospital
Prior experience as a ward nurse

questions.correctOptionText: Occupational health clearance, including immunisation and screening records, and mandatory training such as infection control

distractorRationale.a: Correct: these protect patients and students before clinical contact.
distractorRationale.b: A surgical technique exam is not a standard prerequisite.
distractorRationale.c: Equipment purchase is not a pre-placement requirement from the host.

questions.explanation: Occupational health clearance and mandatory training are standard conditions because they protect patients from infection and prepare you to work safely. The details follow your medical school and host organisation.

questions.stem: A student discovers their hepatitis B vaccination course is incomplete three weeks before placement. What is the most appropriate action?

options.text: Contact occupational health straight away to arrange the remaining doses and ask whether the placement can proceed
Say nothing and hope it is not checked
Write on the form that the course is complete
Cancel the placement without telling anyone

questions.correctOptionText: Contact occupational health straight away to arrange the remaining doses and ask whether the placement can proceed

distractorRationale.a: Correct: early, honest contact gives the best chance of resolution.
distractorRationale.b: Concealment is unprofessional and risks patient safety.
distractorRationale.d: Cancelling without communication affects others and may not be necessary.

questions.explanation: Occupational health can advise on timing and any restrictions, but only if you tell them early. Honesty about requirements is part of professional behaviour.

questions.stem: Which question is best for making use of a busy consultant's time during a clinic?

options.text: 'For the patient just seen, what made you choose an inhaler rather than a tablet, and what would change your mind?'
'Can you teach me everything about lung disease?'
'Do you mind if I ask lots of questions later?'
'Is there anything I should know?'

questions.correctOptionText: 'For the patient just seen, what made you choose an inhaler rather than a tablet, and what would change your mind?'

distractorRationale.a: Correct: specific, tied to a case, and about reasoning.
distractorRationale.b: Far too broad to answer in a clinic.
distractorRationale.c: Does not state a question or timing.
distractorRationale.d: Too vague to prompt a useful answer.

questions.explanation: Specific questions anchored in a real case focus the answer on clinical reasoning and can be answered quickly. Broad questions need long explanations that a busy clinic cannot offer.

questions.stem: You have six questions for your supervisor but only 10 minutes at the end of the day. What is the best approach?

options.text: Choose the two or three most important questions, direct practical ones to the nurse or administrator, and say what you already think the answer is
Ask all six in a rapid list without background
Interrupt the next consultation to ask the most urgent one
Do not ask any questions to avoid being a burden

questions.correctOptionText: Choose the two or three most important questions, direct practical ones to the nurse or administrator, and say what you already think the answer is

distractorRationale.a: Correct: prioritising, delegating practical queries and showing prior thinking uses time well.
distractorRationale.b: A rapid list gives little depth and wastes time.

questions.explanation: Prioritisation and choosing the right person make the best use of limited time. Showing your own reasoning lets the supervisor correct and extend it efficiently.

questions.stem: True or false: if you are well prepared on the day, it does not matter whether your mandatory training and clearance were completed before the placement started.

options.text: True
False

questions.explanation: Clearance and mandatory training protect patients and you and are usually conditions of patient contact, so you may be refused access without them. They are not replaced by personal preparation.

questions.stem: A student says that their goal for a one-week elderly care placement is 'to learn about older people'. Rewrite this as two SMART goals and explain how each meets the SMART criteria.
markingGuide: Goal 1 is specific and has a clear output, such as taking and presenting a history from two older patients
Goal 2 differs in type, for example knowledge such as describing how a falls assessment is done, or a professional behaviour
Each goal has a measure of success, such as a number of tasks or feedback received
Each goal has a deadline within the placement
Each is achievable and relevant to course outcomes and the setting
Mentions sharing the goals with the supervisor and reviewing them
questions.explanation: SMART goals translate a broad interest into tasks that can be done, observed and reviewed within the time available. Sharing them with a supervisor makes it more likely they can be met.

questions.stem: List the main occupational health and mandatory training requirements to complete before clinical contact on a UK placement, and explain why each matters.
markingGuide: Occupational health clearance and health questionnaire: fitness and safety for patients and student
Immunisations and screening such as hepatitis B, MMR, varicella and tuberculosis assessment, with blood-borne virus screening before exposure-prone procedures
Disclosure and barring check: safeguarding vulnerable patients
Mandatory training in infection control, manual handling, fire safety, information governance, safeguarding and basic life support where required
ID badge, dress code and local induction
Notes that exact requirements follow the medical school and host organisation and that early completion avoids missing placement time
questions.explanation: Each requirement manages a specific risk, such as infection transmission, safeguarding or confidentiality. Completing them early protects patients and keeps the placement on schedule.

questions.stem: Describe how you would prepare questions for a supervising clinician in a busy surgical clinic so that you use their time well, and give two examples of good questions.
markingGuide: Reads about common conditions beforehand and notes gaps in understanding
Writes questions down and prioritises the two or three most valuable
Asks specific open questions about reasoning, not broad topic requests
Chooses suitable timing: not during consultations or urgent tasks, or asks for a short slot at the end
Directs practical or administrative questions to appropriate staff
Shares own understanding first so the supervisor can confirm or correct
Two clear example questions linked to cases in clinic
questions.explanation: Prepared, prioritised and specific questions make teaching efficient, and showing prior thinking invites correction rather than a lecture. Timing and choosing the right person respect the clinic's priorities.
